'''רעידת האדמה במזרח הקרוב בשנת 1068''' הייתה [[רעידת אדמה]] שהתרחשה בבוקר של ה-[[18 במרץ]] [[1068]] באזור [[המזרח הקרוב]]. רעידת האדמה גרמה לכ-20,000 מקרי מוות ולנזקים מהותיים ב[[מצרים]], ב[[ארץ ישראל]], ב[[חצי האי ערב]], ובאזורים אחרים ממזרח ל[[הים התיכון|ים התיכון]]. ההערכה היא שרעידת האדמה הייתה בעוצמה 7.0 ב[[סולם מגניטודה לפי מומנט]].

== נזקים מרעידת האדמה ==
האזור הצפוני ביותר בו הורגשה רעידת האדמה היה היישוב [[בניאס (סוריה)|בניאס]] (שנמצא בעת המודרנית באזור חוף הים של [[סוריה]]) והאזור הדרומי ביותר בו הורגשה רעידת האדמה היה אזור [[חג'אז]] (שנמצא בעת המודרנית ב[[ערב הסעודית]]). ה[[עיר עתיקה|עיר העתיקה]] של "איילה", הממוקמת בקצה הצפוני של [[מפרץ אילת]], בה נמצאת בעת המודרנית העיר [[עקבה]], נחרבה לחלוטין.

בנוסף לכך רעידת האדמה גרמה גם נזק לעיר העתיקה [[תיניס]] שבמצרים. ב[[קהיר]] הנזק היחיד שגרמה רעידת האדמה היה נזק ל[[מסגד עומר אבן אל-אס]] {{אנ|Amr ibn al-As Mosque}}. לפי ההערכות של ה[[סייסמולוג]] ניקולס אמברסיס רעידת האדמה גרמה לנזקים רבים במיוחד ב[[רמאללה]] שם להערכתו היו בסביבות 15,000 מקרי מוות.

Two major [[earthquakes]] occurred in the [[Near East]] on 18 March and 29 May, AD 1068. The two earthquakes are often amalgamated by contemporary sources.<ref name=Ambraseys/> The first earthquake had its [[epicentre]] somewhere in the northwestern part of the [[Arabian Peninsula]] around [[Tabuk, Saudi Arabia|Tabuk]], while the second was most damaging in the city of [[Ramla]] in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]], some 500 km to the northwest.<ref name=Ambraseys/>

The March earthquake affected the southern portion of the [[Dead Sea Transform]] (DST) [[Fault (geology)|fault]] system. The combined events were responsible for an estimated 20,000 deaths, of which some 15,000 occurred in Ramla alone, and caused damage throughout [[Bilad ash-Sham|Greater Syria]], including Palestine, where a [[tsunami]] devastated the [[Mediterranean]] coast, in [[Egypt]] and the [[Arabian Peninsula]], and in areas to the east along the [[Euphrates]] such as [[al-Rahba]] and [[Kufa]].<ref name=Ambraseys/> Other strong earthquakes have occurred in the southern portion of the DST throughout history, impacting the wider region.

==Geological setting==
The [[Dead Sea Transform]] (DST) is a {{convert|1000|km|abbr=on}} transform fault that spans from the [[Red Sea]] in the south to the [[East Anatolian Fault]] in Turkey to the north. The southern extent of the DST is known as the Wadi Araba fault (after the [[Arabah]] valley). This portion of the DST runs {{convert|160|km|sp=us}} from north of [[Aqaba]]/[[Eilat]] to south of the [[Dead Sea]] and has a slip rate of 4 mm ±2 mm per year.<ref name=yeats>{{citation|title=Active Faults of the World|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aQUgAwAAQBAJ|last=Yeats|first=R.|year=2012|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|isbn=978-0521190855|pages=293, 294, 296}}</ref> The temporal pattern of large events has not been clarified yet, with only four well-documented large earthquakes reported in the Araba valley over the last few thousands of years occurring in 1068, 1212, 1293 and 1458 [[Common Era|CE]].<ref name=Klinger/>

In 1998, Zilberman thought to locate the epicentre of the 1068 event at the [[Dead Sea Transform#Wadi Arabah|Avrona]] [[endorheic basin|playa]], i.e. in the southern part of the Arava Valley.<ref>Zilberman, Ezra; Amit, Rivka; Porat, Naomi; Enzel, Yehouda. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235346183_Surface_ruptures_induced_by_the_devastating_1068_AD_earthquake_in_the_southern_Arava_valley_Dead_Sea_Rift_Israel Surface ruptures induced by the devastating 1068 AD earthquake in the southern Arava valley, Dead Sea Rift, Israel]. ''Tectonophysics'' 408(1–4):79–99 (abstract), October 2005, {{doi|10.1016/j.tecto.2005.05.030}}. Accessed 22 August 2020.</ref><ref>Klinger (2005), see References: Zilberman E. et al. (1998)</ref> Ambraseys (2005) separates between a March event with the epicentre near Tabuk, and a May event closer to Ramla.<ref name=Ambraseys/>

==Effects==
The earthquake's effects were seen from as far north as [[Banias]] at the southern foot of [[Mount Hermon]], to the [[Hejaz]] region of modern-day [[Saudi Arabia]]. The ancient city of [[Ayla (city)|Ayla]], located at the northern end of the [[Gulf of Aqaba]] where modern Aqaba stands today, was destroyed. [[Paleoseismology|Palaeoseismic]] investigations have revealed more than {{convert|12|km|sp=us}} of fault rupture, beginning just north of Aqaba/Eilat, that were dated between 900 and 1,000 [[years before present]]. A magnitude of at least 7.0 was presented based on the reported damage and the extent of the observed fault breaks.<ref name=Klinger>{{cite journal|first1=Y. |last1=Klinger |first2=J. P. |last2=Avoua |first3=L. |last3=Dorbath |first4=N. |last4=Abou Karaki |first5=N. |last5=Tisnerat |title=Seismic behaviour of the Dead Sea fault along the Araba valley, Jordan |journal=[[Geophysical Journal International]] |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |volume=142 |issue=3 |year=2000 |page=772 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-246x.2000.00166.x |bibcode=2000GeoJI.142..769K |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Alarm was caused at [[Saint Catherine's Monastery]] on the [[Sinai Peninsula]], and there was damage in the ancient city of [[Tennis, Egypt|Tinnis]] in the [[Nile Delta]], but not farther to the west along the Egyptian coast in [[Alexandria]]. In [[Cairo]] the only damage was to a corner of the [[Mosque of Amr ibn al-As]] in [[Fustat]]. Seismologist [[Nicholas Ambraseys]] described one account of the effects at [[Ramla]] as destructive and with a large loss of life (15,000 deaths, 200 of which were boys at a school). He also expounded on the effects to the north in Banias, where 100 were killed, and in [[Jerusalem]], where the roof of the [[Dome of the Rock]] was "displaced and then returned to its former position". Those that were affected by the heavy damage in Ramla apparently migrated to Jerusalem, which indicated to Ambraseys that the effects there were otherwise minimal.<ref name=Ambraseys>{{cite book |title= The Seismicity of Egypt, Arabia and the Red Sea: A Historical Review |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=fxnnk2inWT0C&pg=PA31 |first1=N. N. |last1= Ambraseys |first2= C. P. |last2= Melville |first3= R. D. |last3= Adams |year= 2005 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn= 978-0-521-02025-1 |pages= 30–32, 101}}</ref>

==Other events==
In addition to the event in 1068, the southern portion of the DST has experienced three other historical events (all having an estimated magnitude of 6.5–7.0) with two in the northern section near the Dead Sea, and one closer to Aqaba. The event in '''1212''' caused significant damage to towns in the Arabah Valley as well as the destruction of a church on the Sinai Peninsula. In '''1293''', near the southern portion of the Dead Sea, an earthquake destroyed three towers of a castle{{dubious|Most likely Karak, is not on the DS shore as the text seems to indicate; no castles there.|date=July 2020}} and caused damage between the Dead Sea and [[Gaza city|Gaza]]. In '''1458''', another event again affected the southern Dead Sea area, this time causing a {{convert|2.2|m|abbr=on}} [[Fault (geology)#Strike-slip faults|left-lateral]] offset at Qasr at-Tilah ("Tilah Castle", a [[Roman Empire|Roman]] or Early [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] square fort, ca. 25 km south of the Dead Sea). The fort was built across the fault and the building that housed the water tank sustained the displacement.<ref name=yeats/>
